Classification of Antiretroviral Drugs

Classification by Mechanism

1. NRTIs (Nucleoside/Nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors): Tenofovir (TDF), Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF), Lamivudine (3TC), Emtricitabine (FTC), Abacavir (ABC), Zidovudine (AZT), Stavudine (d4T), Didanosine (ddI) — competitive inhibitors of RT; chain terminators (lack 3'-OH).

2. NNRTIs (Non-Nucleoside RT Inhibitors): Efavirenz (EFV), Nevirapine (NVP), Rilpivirine (RPV), Doravirine (DOR), Etravirine (ETR) — non-competitive binding to RT → conformational change → inactivation.

3. PIs (Protease Inhibitors): Atazanavir (ATV), Darunavir (DRV), Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r), Saquinavir, Fosamprenavir — inhibit HIV protease → immature, non-infectious virions.

4. INSTIs (Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors): Dolutegravir (DTG), Bictegravir (BIC), Raltegravir (RAL), Elvitegravir (EVG) — inhibit HIV integrase → prevent viral DNA integration into host genome. Preferred first-line (DTG, BIC).

5. Entry/Attachment Inhibitors: Maraviroc (CCR5 antagonist — requires tropism testing); Enfuvirtide (fusion inhibitor — gp41; SC injection); Ibalizumab (CD4 monoclonal; post-attachment); Fostemsavir (gp120 attachment inhibitor).

6. Capsid inhibitor: Lenacapavir (twice-yearly SC injection — revolutionary long-acting).

Mechanism of Three Drugs

Tenofovir (NRTI): Phosphorylated to tenofovir diphosphate → competes with dATP for RT → incorporated into growing DNA chain → chain termination (no 3'-OH for next nucleotide).

Dolutegravir (INSTI): Binds to active site of HIV integrase → blocks strand transfer (ST) reaction → prevents integration of viral DNA into host chromosome → no proviral DNA formation → no viral replication.

Darunavir (PI): Mimics natural substrate of HIV protease → binds to active site (aspartyl protease) → prevents cleavage of gag-pol polyprotein → produces immature, non-infectious virions. Boosted with ritonavir (CYP3A4 inhibitor) → ↑ darunavir levels.

First-Line ART (WHO 2021)

TLD: Tenofovir (TDF) + Lamivudine (3TC) + Dolutegravir (DTG) — single tablet, once daily. Preferred globally. India's NACP uses TLD as first-line.

Clinical Pearl

INSTIs (especially DTG) are now preferred first-line — high barrier to resistance, well-tolerated, once daily, fewer interactions than PIs/EFV. TLD regimen (TDF+3TC+DTG) is WHO & India NACP first-line. Long-acting injectable ART — cabotegravir + rilpivirine monthly/bimonthly IM (FDA-approved 2021); lenacapavir (twice-yearly SC — revolutionary for adherence). PrEP — TDF/FTC daily or on-demand (2-1-1); long-acting cabotegravir every 2 months (approved 2021). India — NACP provides free ART; TLD first-line; viral load monitoring; ~2.4 million people on ART.

Adverse Effects & Contraindications of Corticosteroids

Adverse Effects

CNS: Psychiatric disturbance (euphoria, insomnia, anxiety, depression, psychosis, mania); pseudotumour cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension).

Musculoskeletal: Osteoporosis (↓ osteoblast, ↑ osteoclast; vertebral fractures; give calcium + vitamin D + bisphosphonate); myopathy (proximal muscle weakness; especially fluoro steroids); avascular necrosis (femoral head).

GI: Peptic ulcer (↑ acid, ↓ mucus; especially with NSAIDs); pancreatitis; GI bleeding/perforation.

Endocrine: Cushingoid features (moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity, striae, acne, hirsutism); hyperglycaemia/diabetes (↑ gluconeogenesis, ↓ insulin sensitivity); HPA suppression (↓ ACTH → adrenal atrophy; abrupt withdrawal → adrenal crisis); menstrual irregularities; growth retardation (children).

Immune: Immunosuppression (↑ infections — bacterial, viral, fungal, reactivation of TB, herpes, hepatitis B); ↓ wound healing; mask signs of infection.

CV: Hypertension (Na & water retention); dyslipidemia; atherosclerosis.

Skin: Thinning, atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, easy bruising, poor wound healing, acne, hirsutism, hyperpigmentation.

Ocular: Cataract (posterior subcapsular); glaucoma (↑ IOP); increased infection risk.

Metabolic: Hyperglycaemia; hypokalaemia; hypernatraemia; fluid retention; weight gain; negative nitrogen/calcium balance.

Contraindications

Active infection (TB, fungal, bacterial, viral — unless life-saving with concurrent antimicrobial); peptic ulcer; osteoporosis; diabetes mellitus; hypertension; heart failure; renal failure; psychiatric illness; glaucoma/cataract; pregnancy (relative — not absolutely contraindicated but use cautiously); live vaccines (immunosuppression).

Clinical Pearl

Always use lowest effective dose for shortest duration. Never stop abruptly — taper gradually (HPA suppression → adrenal crisis on withdrawal). Give in morning (mimics physiological cortisol rhythm; ↓ HPA suppression). Alternate-day dosing — reduces HPA suppression & growth retardation in children. Co-prescribe: calcium + vitamin D (osteoporosis); bisphosphonate (long-term >3 months); PPI (if concurrent NSAID); potassium supplement (if hypokalaemia). Double the dose during stress (illness, surgery — "stress dose steroids"). Always consider steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate, biologics) for chronic conditions. Inhaler/oral rinse after ICS — prevents oral candidiasis.
q2_1_1_2:
Treatment of Diarrhoea

Principles

(1) Rehydration (most important — saves lives); (2) Nutritional support; (3) Symptomatic treatment; (4) Specific antimicrobial (selected cases); (5) Zinc supplementation (children).

1. Rehydration

ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) — WHO formula: Na 75, K 20, Cl 65, citrate 10, glucose 75 mmol/L; osmolarity 245 mOsm/L (hypo-osmolar — better absorption, less stool output). For mild-moderate dehydration. IV fluids (Ringer's lactate) — for severe dehydration, shock, vomiting.

2. Zinc Supplementation

20 mg/day × 10-14 days (children <5 yr); reduces duration, severity, & future episodes; WHO recommended.

3. Symptomatic Treatment

Antimotility: Loperamide 4 mg loading then 2 mg after each loose stool (max 16 mg/day); avoid in children <2 yr, infectious/bloody diarrhoea, C. difficile. Bismuth subsalicylate: antisecretory + antimicrobial; traveller's diarrhoea.

4. Specific Antimicrobials (Selected Cases)

  • Acute watery diarrhoea (viral): no antibiotics; self-limited.
  • Invasive (bloody/mucoid): Shigella — ciprofloxacin/azithromycin; Campylobacter — azithromycin; Salmonella (non-typhoidal) — only if severe/septicaemia; EHEC O157:H7 — avoid antibiotics (↑ HUS risk).
  • Cholera: doxycycline 300 mg single dose; azithromycin.
  • Traveller's diarrhoea: ciprofloxacin/azithromycin/rifaximin × 1-3 days.
  • C. difficile: oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin; stop offending antibiotic.
  • Giardia: metronidazole/tinidazole.
  • Amoebic dysentery: metronidazole/tinidazole + luminal amoebicide (paromomycin/diloxanide).

5. Probiotics

Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Saccharomyces boulardii — reduce duration of acute infectious diarrhoea by ~1 day; especially antibiotic-associated.

6. Diet

Continue feeding (do not starve); BRAT diet (banana, rice, apple sauce, toast) — mild; avoid lactose (transient lactase deficiency), high-sugar/fat foods; breastfeed (continue in infants).

Clinical Pearl

ORS is the single most important intervention — saves millions of lives globally. Avoid antimotility agents in children <2 yr and in bloody/infectious diarrhoea (toxic megacolon risk). Always give zinc to children — reduces duration & future episodes. India — diarrhoea is leading cause of child mortality; ORS + zinc widely available through NTEP/Ayushman Bharat; irrational antibiotic use common; antimicrobial stewardship needed. Rota virus vaccine in UIP (2016) — reduces rotavirus diarrhoea mortality by ~50%.

Complications of General & Spinal Anaesthesia

General Anaesthesia Complications

Immediate (intra-operative): Hypotension; hypertension; arrhythmias; bronchospasm; laryngospasm; hypoxia; hypercapnia; awareness under anaesthesia; malignant hyperthermia (RyR1 mutation; dantrolene); anaphylaxis (neuromuscular blockers, latex, antibiotics); aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome); airway trauma (teeth, lips, vocal cords); endobronchial intubation; oesophageal intubation; equipment failure.

Post-operative: PONV (post-operative nausea & vomiting — most common; 5-HT3 antagonist + dexamethasone + droperidol); shivering (meperidine/clonidine); emergence delirium (especially children; propofol, sevoflurane); delayed emergence (residual anaesthesia, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, stroke); sore throat (intubation); hoarseness; corneal abrasion; pressure injuries; nerve injuries (positioning); urinary retention; DVT/PE (prophylaxis); atelectasis; pneumonia; cognitive dysfunction (POCD — elderly; delirium).

Spinal Anaesthesia Complications

Common/Immediate: Hypotension (sympathetic block — most common; treat with fluids + vasopressors — ephedrine, phenylephrine); bradycardia (high block → vagal unopposed; atropine); nausea/vomising (hypotension or vagal); urinary retention (S2-S4 block — catheterize).

Less common: High/total spinal block (respiratory arrest, unconsciousness — ventilate, vasopressors); subdural block (patchy, slow onset); intravascular injection (systemic toxicity — CNS & CV); post-dural puncture headache (PDPH — CSF leak; onset 24-48h; worse upright, better lying; treatment — hydration, caffeine, NSAIDs, epidural blood patch); backache; transient neurological symptoms (TNS — pain in buttocks/thighs; resolves in days; more with lidocaine).

Rare/Serious: Spinal epidural/subdural haematoma (bleeding disorder/anticoagulants; surgical emergency); abscess (infection; surgical drainage); meningitis/arachnoiditis (infection/chemical); anterior spinal artery syndrome (hypotension + atherosclerosis); cauda equina syndrome (neurological injury); adhesive arachnoiditis (chronic); permanent neurological damage.

Contraindications to spinal: Patient refusal; coagulopathy (INR >1.4, platelets <75,000, on anticoagulants); infection at injection site; sepsis; raised ICP; severe aortic/mitral stenosis; severe hypovolaemia; fixed cardiac output states.

Clinical Pearl

Hypotension is the most common complication of spinal anaesthesia — sympathetic blockade (T4-T6 for abdominal surgery); treat with IV fluids + vasopressors (ephedrine 5-10 mg IV — alpha+beta; phenylephrine 50-100 µg IV — pure alpha1). PDPH — characteristic postural headache (worse sitting/standing, better lying); treat conservatively first (hydration, caffeine, NSAIDs); if persistent >24-48h → epidural blood patch (autologous blood injected into epidural space — seals CSF leak; 70-90% success). Avoid spinal in coagulopathy/anticoagulation — risk of epidural haematoma (surgical emergency → paralysis if not decompressed within 8h). Malignant hyperthermia — stop triggering agent; dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV; hyperventilate 100% O2; cool; treat hyperkalaemia.

ACT (Artemisinin-based Combination Therapy) in Malaria

Definition

ACT — combination of an artemisinin derivative (rapid acting, reduces parasite biomass quickly) + a longer-acting partner drug (eliminates remaining parasites; prevents resistance).

Rationale

  1. Synergy — artemisinin rapidly kills 10^4-10^5 parasites per cycle (within 48h); partner drug eliminates remaining parasites.
  2. Prevent resistance — two drugs with different mechanisms → ↓ probability of simultaneous resistance mutation.
  3. Shorter course — 3 days (vs 7 days monotherapy).
  4. ↓ Gametocyte carriage — artemisinin reduces gametocytes → ↓ transmission.
  5. WHO recommends ACT as first-line for uncomplicated falciparum malaria globally.

WHO-Approved ACTs

  • Artemether + lumefantrine (Coartem) — most widely used; 6 doses over 3 days.
  • Artesunate + amodiaquine.
  • Artesunate + mefloquine.
  • Artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine.
  • Dihydroartemisinin + piperaquine.

Mechanism of Artemisinin

Artemisinin contains endoperoxide bridge → cleaved by haem iron (from digested haemoglobin) → generates free radicals → alkylates parasite proteins & lipids → parasite death. Selective for parasite (which digests haemoglobin) vs host cells.

Clinical Pearl

ACT is WHO first-line for uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria — 3-day course; reduces treatment failure, gametocyte carriage, transmission. Artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) — most widely used; take with fatty food (↑ absorption). For severe malaria — IV artesunate (not ACT) → 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24h; switch to ACT when oral tolerated. India NVBDCP: ACT ( artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine) for P. falciparum; chloroquine for P. vivax (chloroquine-sensitive in most of India). Artemisinin resistance — emerging in Greater Mekong subregion (Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Vietnam, Thailand); delayed parasite clearance; threatens global malaria control; K13 gene mutations; ACTs still effective in Africa & India.
q2_1_1_5:
Chloramphenicol

Mechanism

Binds to 50S ribosomal subunit (overlapping peptidyl transferase centre) → inhibits peptidyl transferase → blocks peptide bond formation → inhibits protein synthesis (bacteriostatic). Same site as macrolides & clindamycin (competitive antagonism — do not combine).

Spectrum

Broad-spectrum — Gram-positive (S. pneumoniae, S. pyogenes, S. aureus, enterococci); Gram-negative (H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, N. gonorrhoeae, Salmonella typhi, Shigella, E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Bacteroides, Vibrio, Yersinia pestis); anaerobes; rickettsiae; spirochaetes; Chlamydia. Inactive against: Pseudomonas, Proteus (some), mycobacteria, fungi, protozoa (except Rickettsia).

Therapeutic Uses (Limited Due to Toxicity)

  • Topical — eye drops/ointment (0.5%) for bacterial conjunctivitis; ear drops for otitis externa. Still commonly used topically in India.
  • Systemic (reserved for serious infections when alternatives unavailable): Typhoid fever (MDR — but ceftriaxone/azithromycin preferred); rickettsial infections (scrub typhus — doxycycline preferred); meningitis (H. influenzae — third-generation cephalosporin preferred); plague; anaerobic infections; VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococcus).
  • Historical — drug of choice for typhoid fever before resistance developed.

Adverse Effects

Bone marrow suppression: (1) Dose-related reversible — ↓ RBC, WBC, platelets (common; dose-related; monitor CBC); (2) Aplastic anaemia (idiosyncratic, irreversible, fatal; 1 in 25,000-40,000; not dose-related; may occur weeks-months after stopping; mechanism — toxic metabolite nitroso-chloramphenicol damages stem cells).

Grey baby syndrome — neonates (especially premature); inability to conjugate (glucuronidation) & excrete chloramphenicol → accumulation → grey skin, hypothermia, cyanosis, hypotonia, cardiovascular collapse, death; contraindicated in neonates.

Other — optic neuritis (long-term); allergic reactions; GI disturbance; disulfiram-like reaction; inhibition of CYP450 (↑ warfarin, phenytoin, tolbutamide, phenobarbital).

Clinical Pearl

Aplastic anaemia is the most feared complication — irreversible, often fatal; idiosyncratic (not dose-related); can occur weeks after stopping; restricted use globally — replaced by safer alternatives (cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones). Grey baby syndrome — neonates lack glucuronyl transferase → drug accumulates → cardiovascular collapse; never give to neonates. India — topical chloramphenicol still widely used (eye drops for conjunctivitis); systemic use rare (reserved for MDR typhoid, rickettsial if doxycycline unavailable). Do NOT combine with macrolides or clindamycin — competitive antagonism at 50S ribosome.
q2_1_1_6:
Rifampicin

Mechanism

Inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (beta-subunit — rpoB gene) → blocks RNA synthesis → bacterial death. Bactericidal. Sterilising action — kills slow-growing & dormant bacilli (unlike isoniazid which kills rapidly multiplying bacilli). Essential for short-course TB therapy (6 months vs 18 months without R).

Spectrum

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (most potent anti-TB drug); M. leprae; Gram-positive (S. aureus including MRSA, S. pneumoniae, enterococci); Gram-negative (N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); Chlamydia; Rickettsia.

Pharmacokinetics

Oral (well absorbed); food ↓ absorption (take on empty stomach); widely distributed (CSF, caseous tissue, macrophages, bone); hepatic metabolism (deacetylation → active metabolite); enterohepatic circulation; excreted in bile, urine, saliva, sweat, tears (orange-red discolouration — normal); half-life 3-5h (shortens with chronic use — autoinduction of CYP).

Therapeutic Uses

  • Tuberculosis — first-line; all categories; essential for 6-month short-course.
  • Leprosy — MB-MDT (monthly rifampicin + daily dapsone + clofazimine).
  • Meningococcal prophylaxis — 600 mg BD × 2 days (close contacts of meningococcal meningitis).
  • Haemophilus influenzae type b prophylaxis — 600 mg daily × 4 days (unvaccinated household contacts <4 yr).
  • Staphylococcal infections — adjunct in prosthetic valve endocarditis, osteomyelitis (with vancomycin); MRSA decolonization.
  • Brucellosis — doxycycline + rifampicin × 6 weeks (alternative to streptomycin).
  • Q fever (Coxiella) — doxycycline + rifampicin/hydroxychloroquine (chronic).

Adverse Effects

  • Hepatotoxicity — dose-related; ↑ with isoniazid + pyrazinamide; monitor LFT (baseline & monthly); stop if ALT >3× ULN with symptoms.
  • Orange-red discolouration — urine, sweat, tears, sputum, stool; stains contact lenses; harmless but alarming — reassure patient.
  • Flu-like syndrome — intermittent dosing (fever, chills, myalgia, rash; switch to daily or reduce dose).
  • Thrombocytopenia — intermittent dosing (immune-mediated).
  • Interstitial nephritis — rare.
  • Gastrointestinal — nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea.
  • Potent CYP3A4 inducer — ↓ levels of MANY drugs: warfarin (↑ INR monitoring), OCPs (use barrier), corticosteroids, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, protease inhibitors (avoid with most PIs — check compatibility), ketoconazole/itraconazole, digoxin, theophylline, phenytoin, propafenone, verapamil, diltiazem, valproate, levothyroxine, haloperidol, methadone, dabigatran, DOACs. Always check ALL medications when starting rifampicin.

Contraindications

Jaundice; severe hepatic dysfunction; hypersensitivity; pregnancy (relative — animal teratogen but used if essential; leprosy — monthly dose considered safe); concurrent use with most protease inhibitors (PIs).

Clinical Pearl

Rifampicin is the most important anti-TB drug — sterilising action; essential for 6-month therapy. Always check drug interactions — potent CYP3A4 inducer; ↓ levels of warfarin, OCPs, steroids, PIs, ciclosporin, many others. Orange urine is normal — reassure patient; warn about contact lenses. Monitor LFT — hepatotoxicity (especially with H+Z). Give on empty stomach (food ↓ absorption). India NTEP: rifampicin 450 mg (<50 kg) or 600 mg (≥50 kg) daily in intensive & continuation phases; fixed-dose combination (HRZE) for adherence.
q2_1_1_7:
Antiseptics and Disinfectants

Definitions

Antiseptic — chemical applied to LIVING tissue (skin, mucous membranes, wounds) to inhibit/kill microorganisms. Disinfectant — chemical applied to INANIMATE objects (surfaces, instruments) to kill microorganisms (not necessarily spores). Sterilant — destroys ALL microbial life including spores.

Classification by Mechanism

  1. Alcohols — Ethanol (70%), Isopropanol (70%); denature proteins, dissolve lipids; rapid (30 sec); no sporicidal; flammable; skin antisepsis, hand hygiene, small instruments.
  2. Halogens:
    • Chlorine compounds — Sodium hypochlorite (0.5-1% for surfaces; 5,000 ppm for blood spills); chloramine; chlorine dioxide; broad-spectrum; inactivated by organic matter; corrosive; water disinfection, surfaces, blood spills.
    • Iodophores — Povidone-iodine (Betadine; 7.5-10%); slow release of iodine; broad-spectrum; skin antisepsis (pre-op scrub, wound care); mucosal (oral, vaginal); inactivated by blood/pus; avoid in neonates (thyroid), iodine allergy.
  3. Phenolics — Phenol, cresol, Lysol, hexachlorophene, chlorhexidine; disrupt cell wall; Chlorhexidine (2% & 4%) — broad-spectrum, persistent (6h), low toxicity; skin antisepsis, oral rinse, hand wash; avoid in neonates (brain toxicity — kernicterus), middle ear (ototoxic).
  4. Quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs) — Benzalkonium chloride, cetrimide; cationic surfactants; disrupt membrane; Gram-positive > Gram-negative; inactivated by soap, anions; skin, instruments, surfaces.
  5. Aldehydes:
    • Glutaraldehyde 2% (Cidex) — high-level disinfectant; sporicidal (10h); sterilises endoscopes, instruments; irritant vapour; 20-45 min HLD.
    • Formaldehyde — 37% formalin (10% = 4% formaldehyde); gas/fumigation; histopathology fixation; carcinogen; irritant.
    • Ortho-phthalaldehyde (OPA) 0.55% — replacement for glutaraldehyde; faster (12 min HLD); less irritant; stains skin/proteins.
  6. Oxidising agents — Hydrogen peroxide (3-6%); peracetic acid (0.2%); ozone; release free radicals; broad-spectrum; sporicidal; environmentally friendly (decompose to water/oxygen).
  7. Heavy metals — Silver nitrate (1% eye drops — historical for neonatal conjunctivitis prophylaxis; Crede prophylaxis); silver sulfadiazine (burns); mercurials (obsolete — toxicity); copper (water purification).
  8. Dyes — Gentian violet (antifungal); acriflavine/proflavine (wounds); eosin; methylene blue.
  9. Gases — Ethylene oxide (EtO; sterilises heat-sensitive items; carcinogen; requires aeration); formaldehyde gas; ozone; hydrogen peroxide vapour/plasma (Sterrad).

Spaulding Classification

Critical (enter sterile tissue) → sterilisation. Semi-critical (contact mucosa) → high-level disinfection. Non-critical (contact intact skin) → intermediate/low-level disinfection.

Clinical Pearl

Alcohol-based handrub (60-80% ethanol/isopropanol) — WHO gold standard for hand hygiene; 20-30 sec; most effective intervention against HAI. Chlorhexidine-alcohol (2% CHG + 70% alcohol) — preferred pre-operative skin prep (persistent activity, broad-spectrum). Povidone-iodine — alternative (especially iodine allergy to CHG; mucosal surfaces). Glutaraldehyde 2% (Cidex) — HLD for endoscopes (20-45 min); discard after 14 days; check MRC strips. Sodium hypochlorite — blood spills (5,000 ppm = 1:10 dilution of 5.25% bleach); surfaces. Ethylene oxide — sterilises heat-sensitive items (catheters, endoscopes); carcinogen; requires aeration 8-12h. India — irrational use of antiseptics/disinfectants common; always follow manufacturer's instructions for contact time, dilution, reuse life; monitor with chemical & biological indicators.
q2_1_1_8:
Albendazole

Mechanism

Binds to beta-tubulin of parasite (selective — much higher affinity than mammalian tubulin) → inhibits microtubule polymerisation → disrupts microtubule-dependent glucose uptake → ↓ glycogen stores → ↓ ATP production → parasite death (energy starvation). Also inhibits fumarate reductase (parasite-specific enzyme in anaerobic metabolism).

Spectrum

Nematodes (roundworms): Ascaris lumbricoides, hookworm (Necator, Ancylostoma), Enterobius (pinworm), Trichuris (whipworm), Strongyloides (less effective — ivermectin preferred), Toxocara (visceral larva migrans), Cutaneous larva migrans, Trichinella.

Cestodes (tapeworms): Taenia solium (neurocysticercosis — drug of choice), Taenia saginata, Hymenolepis nana, Echinococcus (hydatid disease — prolonged course).

Trematodes: Less effective; praziquantel preferred for most flukes.

Others: Giardia lamblia (alternative to metronidazole); Microsporidium; Capillaria.

Pharmacokinetics

Oral; poor absorption (<5%) — take with fatty food (↑ absorption 5×); hepatic metabolism to active sulfoxide metabolite; widely distributed (CSF, hydatid cysts); half-life 8-12h; excreted in bile & urine.

Therapeutic Uses & Doses

  • Intestinal nematodes (Ascaris, hookworm, Enterobius, Trichuris): 400 mg single dose (adults & children >2 yr); repeat after 2-3 weeks for Enterobius.
  • Neurocysticercosis: 15 mg/kg/day (max 1200 mg/day) in 2 divided doses × 7-14 days (with corticosteroids & anticonvulsants).
  • Hydatid disease (Echinococcus): 10-15 mg/kg/day × 1-6 months (pre & post-surgical; or PAIR procedure).
  • Cutaneous larva migrans: 400 mg daily × 3-7 days.
  • Toxocariasis (visceral larva migrans): 400 mg BD × 5 days.
  • Giardiasis: 400 mg daily × 5 days (alternative to metronidazole).
  • Capillariasis: 400 mg daily × 10 days.
  • Mass drug administration (MDA): School-based deworming — 400 mg single dose every 6-12 months for STH control in endemic areas.

Adverse Effects

Generally well-tolerated at single-dose (intestinal helminths): GI (nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea); headache; dizziness; transient ↑ liver enzymes. High doses/prolonged (cysticercosis, hydatid): hepatotoxicity; alopecia; bone marrow suppression (↓ WBC, platelets — monitor CBC); rash; fever; neurological deterioration in neurocysticercosis (inflammatory reaction to dying parasites — always give corticosteroids before & during albendazole).

Contraindications

Pregnancy (teratogenic in animals — avoid especially 1st trimester); ocular cysticercosis (blindness from inflammatory reaction — surgical removal); spinal cord cysticercosis (risk of paralysis — surgical). Caution: hepatic impairment; renal impairment; monitor LFT & CBC during prolonged therapy.

Clinical Pearl

Albendazole is the drug of choice for neurocysticercosis — 15 mg/kg/day × 7-14 days; always give corticosteroids (dexamethasone) before & during therapy to prevent inflammatory reaction to dying cysticerci (oedema → raised ICP → seizures, encephalitis). Avoid in ocular/spinal cysticercosis — inflammation can cause irreversible blindness/paralysis; surgical removal preferred. Take with fatty food — ↑ absorption 5× (poorly absorbed otherwise). Single-dose 400 mg for intestinal helminths — safe, effective, cheap; ideal for mass drug administration (school deworming). India — school-based deworming programme (National Deworming Day — albendazole 400 mg single dose to all children 1-19 years, twice yearly). Mebendazole — alternative (100 mg BD × 3 days or 500 mg single dose); less systemic absorption; preferred for intestinal worms where systemic effect not needed.
